title: Load balancers
summary: Send requests across healthy servers with a load balancer. Trace round-robin routing and see why shared state and useful health checks matter.
introduction: A helper at the library door sends each learner to an open desk. A load balancer does a similar job for requests. It chooses an available server so one server does not have to handle every visitor.
learningObjectives: Describe what a load balancer does
Trace round-robin routing over healthy servers
Explain why a health check cannot guarantee every request succeeds

blocks.text: A **load balancer** receives requests and forwards them to app servers. **Round robin** means taking turns: A, then B, then A again. Other rules can choose the server with fewer active requests.
A **health check** asks whether a server is ready to do useful work. It might test a small readiness endpoint. A machine can answer a network ping while its app is still broken.

The servers need the same important records and compatible code. If a draft exists only in server A's memory, a later request sent to B may not find it. Shared durable state, or carefully designed routing, avoids that surprise.

items: Start with servers A, B, and C. In this example, B is marked unhealthy.
Build a list containing only A and C.
Send four requests to those two servers in turn.
If no server is healthy, return a clear temporary-unavailable result instead of selecting a missing server.

blocks.text: This small JavaScript model runs in the playground. Its numbers and events are chosen for learning. It does not create servers or measure a real service.

blocks.alt: The load balancer skips offline server B and sends requests to A or C. The healthy servers share a database.
blocks.caption: Server B is offline, so requests use A and C. Both still share a database; that part can become a bottleneck.

blocks.text: The percent sign gets the remainder after division. Here it cycles between index 0 and index 1. The code is a routing model; it does not contact servers.
Round robin gives equal request counts here, not necessarily equal work. One search might be cheap while another needs a large report. A routing rule should suit the workload.

rows: Equal counts may hide very different request costs
Can help when requests take different times
Can keep a user on one server for a while
That server may fail, so this is not a backup for important state

blocks.text: A server may fail just after a successful health check. Requests still need time limits and clear errors. Retry only when repeating the action is safe.
The load balancer itself also needs a failure plan. Real services often use redundant managed routing or several balancers. Adding a single new box is not a promise of continuous service.

items: Set B to healthy: true. Predict the targets of four requests.
They become A, B, C, A. Then set all three servers to false and check that every result is unavailable.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not treat a green health check as proof that every future request will work. Checks describe a recent moment and only the parts they test.
